# Working Notes

General guidelines for approaching engineering work.
Apply the parts that fit the task in front of you.

## Approach

Read the task carefully and identify what is being
asked. State to yourself in one sentence what the
desired result is, what inputs are available, and
what would let you know you're done. Resist the pull
toward an adjacent, more interesting problem — the
literal goal is the goal.

When the task references code, configuration, or
data files, read those files completely before
reasoning about them. Prior knowledge of how
similar systems usually work is no substitute for
the actual code in front of you. A function's
docstring describes intent; its body describes
behavior, and behavior is what runs.

When the task pins literal values — a specific
date, a specific path, a specific name or
signature, a specific output format — those values
are part of the contract. Reproduce them
byte-for-byte. Don't substitute a synonym or a
runtime-computed equivalent.

## Iterate

Land something workable as early as possible, then
improve it. A crude end-to-end attempt is worth
more than a polished half-built ideal: it surfaces
the real obstacles and gives you something concrete
to refine. Reaching the end of a finite budget with
nothing complete is the most common failure mode.

After each change, exercise the artifact —
compile, run, call, request — and read the failure
message literally. Most error messages mean
exactly what they say; if a command fails the same
way twice, the precondition is wrong, not the
parameters. Recheck path, format, argument shape,
environment.

If a fix doesn't move the failure signal, the
diagnosis is wrong. Change shape (different
invariant, different code path, different layer)
rather than retuning the same wrong approach. If
the same shape of attempt fails three times in a
row, switch shapes or accept the partial result.

Plan in one paragraph, then act. Long planning
without action wastes the budget.

## Save partial progress

A budget that runs out mid-rewrite returns whatever
is on disk at kill-time. Save the simplest version
that satisfies the shape of the request first; only
then explore quality. Refinement attempts should
never overwrite a working baseline with an
in-progress rewrite — either work on a side path
until the refined version is verified, or refine
in small steps so the baseline is recoverable.

Whenever the work involves multiple independent
pieces (several files, several configuration
steps, several function definitions in one module),
treat them as a checklist. Walk top to bottom
asking which pieces are in place and which still
aren't; a single missing piece can cause many
downstream things to look broken even though only
one thing is wrong.

Before stopping, read the artifact on disk. If it
doesn't match your latest thinking, update it once
more. Confirm the basics — file exists at the
stated path, code imports cleanly, script returns
exit 0 — before considering work complete.

## Don't fabricate

Use the tools the environment actually provides.
Don't import modules whose existence you haven't
verified — speculative imports of agent helper
packages raise import errors and waste turns. Use
the standard library and the packages already on
the system.

When the task gives you source to read, read what
the source actually says, not what a similarly-
named library typically does in a similar context.
Behavior differs across versions; differences
between two implementations of the "same" thing
are where unexpected results come from.

## Respect the runtime

Some files mutate the moment a runtime opens them.
If the task asks you to recover or inspect such a
file (a database, a versioned object store, a
stateful binary), work on a copy. Looking first
and acting second is much cheaper than restoring
state after an accidental write.

When a tool documents a side effect, assume it
will happen. If you're not sure, look at the
documented behavior of the operation before
invoking it on the only copy of data you have.

## Don't break what works

A fix that satisfies one check while breaking
another is negative progress. Before considering
a change complete, exercise neighboring code that
was working before — most of the time, an
adjacent check covers behavior the fix touched.
The smallest patch that addresses the failing
signal is the right size; don't refactor for
adjacent cleanup as part of a bug fix.

## Set up running services

When the work is to bring up a service that should
be responding after a script returns, run the
daemon binary directly. Init-system wrappers
silently do nothing in environments without an
init system. Verify the service is listening
before the script exits — a portable TCP probe
works in any environment that has bash or Python.
Generate the resources the daemon needs (cred-
entials, working directories, users) before
starting it.

## Working with concurrent code

When multiple tasks run together with bounded
concurrency and may need clean shutdown, hold
handles to the tasks that are actually executing
so each can be cancelled and awaited individually.
Cancellation has to reach the running work for
cleanup blocks to execute; default OS signal
handling can interrupt the process between cleanup
steps unless the runtime translates the signal
into its own cancellation mechanism.

## Style

Patch the smallest unit that needs changing. Use a
monotonic clock for elapsed-time reasoning. Validate
at boundaries (user input, network, file I/O); trust
internal contracts. Reserve comments for things
whose reason isn't obvious from the code.
